segments.text: Which way does a Persian line run? Say yek.

blocks.title: Script — the shapes, and the direction

segments.text: ۰ — sefr, zero ۱ — yek, one.
Persian has its own ten digit signs, and every price ticket, telephone number and page number in Iran is written in them. A reader who can say yek and cannot read ۱ still cannot read a price.
۰ is a dot, not a ring. Fix that first, because a European eye reads a dot as a decimal point — and Persian's nine is the ring.

Now the part no earlier chapter has had to say: numbers run left to right, inside a line that runs right to left. Ten is ۱۰ — one, then zero, in the European order — while the words around it move the other way. The page changes direction at the number and changes back after it.
Sources: Unicode Arabic chart; Omniglot, Numbers in Persian.

segments.prompt: A Persian line runs right to left. Which way do the digits inside it run?
acceptedResponses: the other way, left to right

feedback.correct: The number is the one place the direction flips.
feedback.incorrect: Left to right — ۱۰ is one then zero.

lessons.title: ۲ ۳ (do se) — one tooth apart
lessons.gloss: two digits that differ by a single tooth

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shapes and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Write ۰ and ۱, then read ۱۰.
۲ — do, two ۳ — se, three.

۳ is ۲ with one more tooth. That is the whole difference, and it is small enough that the two have to be written as a pair rather than one at a time — say do and se aloud as the hand makes them and the shapes stop competing.
Sources: Unicode Arabic chart; Omniglot, Numbers in Persian.

segments.prompt: Write the Persian digit for three, then the digit for two.

feedback.incorrect: Three first, then two — three is two plus a tooth.

lessons.title: ۴ ۵ ۶ (chahâr panj shesh) — the three Persian keeps for itself
lessons.gloss: the three digits Persian draws differently from Arabic

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shapes and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Write ۲ and ۳, and say which has the extra tooth.
۴ — chahâr, four ۵ — panj, five ۶ — shesh, six.
These three are the reason this chapter exists as more than a list.

Seven of the ten digits are drawn the same way in Persian and in Arabic. ۴, ۵ and ۶ are not: Arabic writes those three with quite different shapes. A reader who picked up the digits from an Arabic book will read an Iranian price wrongly at exactly these three places and nowhere else.
If you drill three of the ten harder than the rest, drill these.
Sources: Unicode Arabic chart; Omniglot, Numbers in Persian.

segments.prompt: Write the three Persian digits that Arabic draws differently.

feedback.correct: Four, five and six — and no others.

lessons.title: ۷ ۸ ۹ (haft hasht noh) — a mirror pair, and the ring
lessons.gloss: a mirror pair, a ring with a tail, and the set is closed

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script — the shapes and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Write ۴, ۵, ۶ — the three Arabic draws differently.
۷ — haft, seven ۸ — hasht, eight ۹ — noh, nine.
۷ and ۸ are mirror images of each other, one opening upward and one downward. Write them as a pair, every time, and the mirror stops being a problem — the same trick that worked on ۲ and ۳.
۹ is a ring with a tail, and this is where a dot-shaped zero pays off. Had ۰ been a ring too, the page would carry two rings and no way to separate them.
Ten signs, four lessons. The set is closed.

segments.source: [YOU WRITE: **۷** and **۸** as a pair, then **۹**]

segments.prompt: Which two Persian digits are mirror images of each other?

feedback.correct: Write them as a pair and they stop competing.

lessons.title: Payoff — reading the figures
lessons.gloss: payoff — a price, a telephone number and a page number, read off the page

segments.text: Count one to twenty, then say which way digits run inside a Persian line.
Read all ten signs shuffled and say each as a Persian word.
Read ۱۰, ۱۱, ۲۰ and ۱۰۰ and say each — dah, yâzdah, bist, sad.
Hear ten amounts named and write each in Persian figures.
Write the ten signs from dictation, out of order, and check ۴, ۵ and ۶ against the models rather than against memory.
Say what a reader can now do that could not be done four chapters ago: read a price, a page number and a telephone number off an Iranian page.
Sources: Unicode Arabic chart; Omniglot, Numbers in Persian.

segments.prompt: Write a hundred in Persian figures.

feedback.correct: One and two zeros, left to right.
feedback.incorrect: ۱ then ۰ then ۰ — the digits run left to right.
